articles.title: Losing childhood weight by adulthood might erase later depression risks
articles.summary: A massive new study shows that while being heavier or thinner than average in childhood is linked to mental health risks, reaching a normal weight by adulthood might erase that excess vulnerability to depression and anxiety.

articles.title: Women don’t find deeper-than-average voices more attractive when they can see the man
articles.summary: When people could see a man’s full body on video, digitally deepening his voice made him seem stronger and more dominant, but not more attractive to women, a study in Royal Society Open Science found.

articles.title: Voters value long-term economic growth more than previously thought, study finds
articles.summary: New research reveals that voters are not simply shortsighted when evaluating the economy. Instead of focusing only on the immediate past, people consistently prefer a steady upward trajectory, even if it means sacrificing overall benefits.

articles.title: Scientists map a blood protein fingerprint of menopause tied to brain health
articles.summary: Blood proteins tied to inflammation, nerve cell connections, and Alzheimer’s biology shift across menopause, and older women with more of this pattern tend to show faster cognitive decline, a multi-cohort study suggests.

articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? How should applied behavioral scientists navigate the financial and political influences on the work

articles.title: Scientists discover new Alzheimer’s drug that repairs DNA damage and reduces brain inflammation
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered that a drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries can tackle several key features of Alzheimer’s disease, including DNA damage and inflammation. Already tested for initial safety in humans, the experimental treatment could offer a faster path toward therapies that target the disease at its roots.

articles.summary: arXiv:2611.05393v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models perform strongly on standard medical QA but degrade on harder reasoning tasks, where multi-agent debate often fails to beat strong single-model prompting. We argue that a key limitation is that existing systems select experts and retrieve knowledge from the question alone, rather than from gaps that emerge during reasoning. articles.title: A minimal E/I circuit model explains differential recovery from amblyopia under TTX and reverse occlusion
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.06189v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recovery from amblyopia beyond the critical period remains a major challenge in visual neuroscience. Experimental studies show that transient inactivation of the fellow eye with tetrodotoxin (TTX) produces stronger and more persistent recovery than reverse occlusion (RO), despite both interventions reducing competition from the fellow eye. The circuit mechanisms underlying this difference remain unclear. We develop a minimal cortical circuit model combining excitatory-inhibitory population dynamics, BCM-like metaplasticity, homeostatic regulation

articles.title: Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired
articles.summary: Scientists propose that the brain’s mysterious cross-wiring, which connects each hemisphere to the opposite side of the body, may have originated more than 500 million years ago in the visual systems of ancient fish. Rather than evolving for a specific advantage, this unusual arrangement may simply be a legacy of evolution building new brain circuits on an ancient foundation.

articles.title: Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success
articles.summary: A massive new study reveals that intelligence plays a surprisingly limited role in children's reading success, while visual processing showed no meaningful connection at all. Instead, the strongest predictors are sound recognition, vocabulary, and background knowledge, offering new clues about how to help struggling readers.

articles.title: The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
articles.summary: A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism could help explain why people with anxiety or PTSD sometimes experience intense fear in completely safe situations.
